spans.content: A Transformer Framework Informed by Muscle
Anatomy and Sequence-to-Sequence
Translation for Continuous Joint
Kinematics Prediction Using sEMG
Zijun Wei , Zhiqiang Zhang , Senior Member, IEEE, and Sheng Quan Xie , Fellow, IEEE
Abstract—The key to achieving assist-as-needed (AAN)
control in rehabilitation robots lies in accurately predict-
ing patient motion intentions. This study, for the first time,
redefines motion intention prediction from the perspec-
tive of sequence-to-sequence translation by analogizing
sEMG signals and joint angles to the source language
and target language, respectively. The proposed 3DCNN-TF
model achieves precise translation of neural control signals
into kinematic representations. This model comprises three
modules: an sEMG “sentence” generation module that
compiles multiple sEMG sliding windows into a “sentence,”
a 3DCNN module based on muscle anatomy and electrode
placement to extract muscle synergy features from each
“word” in the “sentence,” and a Transformer (TF) module
that autoregressively generates the next joint angle as the
translation result. Experimental results indicate that the
3DCNN-TF model achieves superior overall performance
compared to eight baseline models and existing studies
in continuously predicting wrist and knee flexion/extension
angles across varying speeds. Moreover, the 3DCNN-TF
achieves an optimal balance between prediction accuracy
and computational efficiency while exhibiting exceptional
robustness and generalizability. Specifically, the 3DCNN-TF
achieves average nRMSE and R<sup>2</sup> values of (6.2% /95.5% )
and (5.5% /96.2% ) on wrist and knee datasets, respectively,
with an average training time of less than two minutes.
Additionally, the 3DCNN-TF can predict joint angles up to
300 ms in advance without compromising accuracy, which
is critical for real-time AAN control in rehabilitation robots.
Index Terms—Surface electromyography (sEMG),
upper-limb rehabilitation, deep learning, muscle anatomy,
sequence-to-sequence, continuous joint kinematics esti-
mation methods.

sis after a stroke, with persistent motor dysfunction in both

intensity, rather than solely relying on robotic assistance. This

tient involvement to induce brain and nervous system remod-
eling. Therefore, developing an “Assist-As-Needed” (AAN)
control strategy that can precisely adjust robotic assistance in
real-time based on patient’s effort levels is crucial. The key
to achieving this lies in the accurate and continuous predic-
tion of patients’ motion intentions [3]. Previous research has
demonstrated that surface electromyography (sEMG), due to
its non-invasive nature and portability, has been widely utilized
to predict motion intentions [4]. Hence, this study will further
investigate the continuous estimation of joint kinematics based
on sEMG.
Based on our systematic review of 186 related studies over
the past decade [4], deep learning (DL) has been extensively
applied for the continuous prediction of joint kinematics and
dynamics using sEMG. DL can automatically extract and select
advanced features from sEMG and utilize the fitting capabilities
of neural networks to establish nonlinear mappings between
these features and motion intentions. The review [4] also high-
lighted that most current DL models focus on hybrid neural
networks that combine convolutional neural networks (CNN),
recurrent neural networks (RNN), and multi-head self-attention
(MSA) mechanisms, such as CNN-BM (CNN-BiLSTM with
MSA). These combinations have demonstrated superior predic-
tion performance compared to models employing only CNNs or
RNNs. Specifically, CNN-BM first extracts spatial features from
sEMG using CNNs, then applies BiLSTM to capture long-term
bidirectional contextual dependencies among these features,
thereby obtaining spatiotemporal representations ofsEMG, with
MSA subsequently employed to enhance the weighting of crit-
ical spatiotemporal features.
However, the attention distribution of MSA only operates on
the spatiotemporal features extracted by BiLSTM, and BiLSTM
still has inherent limitations due to its recurrent structure, such
as limited ability to remember long-range contextual relations,
the risk of gradient vanishing or explosion during training, and
lack of parallel computing [4], [5]. In contrast, the Transformer
(TF) model overcomes these limitations. TF can simultaneously
capture contextual relationships across all positions in the se-
quence without depending on sequential order, which makes it
insensitive to temporal distance. Therefore, in the latest studies,
TF and its variant BERT have replaced BiLSTM [4], [5], [6].
However, according to all relevant literature retrieved from
PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore [5], [6],
except for studies [7], [17], and [18], most studies have only
employed the TF encoder (TFE) for the continuous estimation
of joint kinematics from sEMG. This approach only exploits
the TFE’s strength in capturing contextual dependencies within
input sequences, overlooking the potential of the TF decoder
(TFD) to generate temporally correlated target sequences based
on the contextual representations provided by TFE.
Furthermore, although studies [7], [17], and [18] employed a
full encoder-decoder framework, they all adopted the Informer
(InF) model, which is a variant of TF [19]. In fact, InF was
designed for long-term time-series forecasting, and its sparse
MSA and distillation operations may lose detailed information
in short sEMG feature sequences, thereby degrading predictive
performance [20]. Additionally, the InF decoder generates the
entire target sequence at once, rather than progressively in an
autoregressive manner. Although this approach can improve
inference speed and capture longer temporal dependencies, the
lack of incremental feedback can lead to error accumulation, as
the model cannot dynamically adjust the output [20]. Given that
the non-stationary nature of sEMG requires precise capturing of
short-term temporal features and high-frequency dynamics, and
considering the sEMG sliding window is a short-time sequence,
InF may not be optimal. Instead, using TFD with full MSA and
autoregressive generation may maximize prediction accuracy.
According to the conclusions in our review, the core con-
cept of DL models should revolve around accurately extracting
spatiotemporal features from sEMG, enhancing the weights of
key features, and deriving causal relationships between inputs
and outputs based on the contextual dependencies among these
features, while filtering out redundant features and noise as much
as possible to improve predictive accuracy and robustness [4].
Additionally, the review emphasizes the importance of extract-
ing muscle synergy (MS) features, which can further eliminate
redundant and noisy components in sEMG due to individual
differences, the time-varying nature of sEMG, and coupling and
crosstalk between agonist and antagonist muscles. Therefore,
based on these conclusions, we adopt CNN-BM as the base
template and improve both CNN and BM modules to achieve
better motion intention prediction performance.
Our recent study [21] on MS feature extraction has improved
the CNN module in CNN-BM from four different perspectives
while keeping the BM module unchanged, demonstrating that
the 3DCNN-BM based on the target muscle anatomy and sEMG
electrode placement achieved the most efficient MS feature
extraction capability and optimal motion intention prediction
performance compared to other methods. Therefore, this study
continues to employ the 3DCNN from study [21] to extract MS
features, with the 3DCNN-BM as one of the baseline models.
Furthermore, the underlying rationale of this study is that,
according to musculoskeletal dynamics and kinematics, sEMG
signals and corresponding joint angles during limb movement
can be viewed as two physiological languages that represent the
same neural control information in different forms. Specifically,
sEMG represents implicit neural commands based on action
potentials, whereas joint angles are the explicit motor outcomes
of muscle contraction, implying a strong causal correspondence
between them. From the perspective of language translation,
using sEMG to predict joint angles resembles simultaneous
interpretation, which requires the model to translate the im-
plicit neural language of sEMG into joint angles as kinematic
expressions. Therefore, this study used sequence-to-sequence
(Seq2Seq) based TF to improve the BM module in 3DCNN-BM,
thereby achieving precise translation from sEMG tojoint angles.
The proposed 3DCNN-TF model consists of three modules:
an sEMG “sentence” generation module that interprets each
sEMG sliding window as a “word” and compiles multiple
“words” into a “sentence” within the allowable prediction la-
tency, a 3DCNN module that extracts MS features from each
“word” in the sEMG “sentence”, and a TF module that pro-
gressively generates the next joint angle as the translation result
based on global contextual dependencies between the MS fea-
ture sequence and the prior joint angle sequence.
Notably, the TF module incorporates five key enhancements
over the conventional TF architecture: an additional segment
encoding is introduced to distinguish the sequential order of
“words” within a “sentence”; the 3DCNN module replaces the
traditional embedding layer in TFE to extract MS features as the
semantic representation of each “word”; an extra causal mask is
integrated into TFD to strictly enforce temporal causality during
next joint angle generation; a dynamic Teacher Forcing strategy
based on Scheduled Sampling [22] is adopted during the au-
toregressive loop training to accelerate model convergence and
mitigate error accumulation; unlike conventional multi-layer
TF designs, both TFE and TFD in the proposed TF module
are single-layer structures, significantly reducing computational
complexity while maintaining predictive performance.
The proposed 3DCNN-TF model was validated on our wrist
joint dataset and the public lower-limb dataset from EPIC
Lab [23]. This model was compared to eight baseline mod-
els (3DCNN-InF, 3DCNN-TFE, 3DCNN-BM, TF, TFE, CNN-
TFE, CNN-BM, and TCN) for predicting wrist and knee flex-
ion/extension angles during level-ground walking at slow, nor-
mal, and fast speeds. Experimental results demonstrated that
the 3DCNN-TF model achieved optimal overall performance,
balancing prediction accuracy and computational efficiency,
while also exhibiting superior generalizability and robustness.

II. MATERIALS
A. IRASS Dataset
This dataset was approved by the MaPS and Engineering
Joint Faculty Research Ethics Committee of the University of
Leeds (MEEC 18-002), involving 12 subjects (8 males and 4
females, aged 28.9 ± 2.8 years) who provided informed consent
and participated in the experiment.
As shown in Fig. 1(a), before the experiment, all subjects
were instructed to maintain an upright posture, with their elbows
flexed at 90 degrees, their shoulders abducted at 90 degrees,
and their hands in a neutral position. Subsequently, the maxi-
mum voluntary contraction (MVC) values for each subject were
recorded to normalize the sEMG signals. During the experiment,
subjects were required to perform continuous wrist flexion and
extension movements, with the metacarpophalangeal (MCP)
joints fully extended while avoiding the wrist ulnar and radial
deviation. Each subject performed five trials, with a three-minute
rest interval between trials to prevent muscle fatigue.
Wrist flexion/extension movements were recorded using the
VICON motion capture system (VICON Motion Systems Ltd.,
U.K.) at a frequency of 250 Hz. According to the VICON
upper limb model, 16 corresponding reflective markers were
placed on the subjects’ right arms, enabling the VICON Nexus
software to calculate the wrist joint flexion/extension angles.
Meanwhile, sEMG signals from two wrist flexors: flexor carpi
radialis (FCR) and flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU), and three wrist
extensors: extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU), extensor carpi radialis
longus (ECRL), and extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB), were
collected using Avanti sensors (Delsys Trigno<sup>TM</sup>) at 2000 Hz.
Moreover, to ensure the quality of sEMG signals, the subjects
forearms were shaved and cleaned with alcohol to minimize
skin impedance and motion artifacts. Electrode placement was
determined according to SENIAM guidelines and confirmed
through palpation and signal quality assessment. Finally, sEMG
data and joint angle data were synchronized using the trigger
module in VICON Nexus software and resampled at 1000 Hz.

C. Signal Preprocessing
Given that the effective frequency range of sEMG signals is
between 20-400 Hz, with components outside this range primar-
ily consisting of motion artifacts and noise [25], a 20-400 Hz
fifth-order Butterworth bandpass filter was first applied to the
sEMG signals in both datasets, followed by a 50 Hz notch filter
to eliminate powerline interference. To obtain smoother sEMG
envelope signals for stable model training and faster conver-
gence, full-wave rectification and a 5 Hz fifth-order Butterworth
low-pass filter were subsequently applied. Finally, since MVC
values were only recorded for the IRASS dataset, sEMG en-
velopes from the IRASS dataset were normalized based on their
respective MVC values, whereas those from the EPIC dataset
were normalized using Z-score normalization. As forjoint angle,
both datasets were smoothed using a fifth-order Butterworth
low-pass filter at 5 Hz, followed by min-max normalization to
linearly scale the wrist and knee joint angle to the ranges of [-1,
1] and [0, 1], respectively.

Given that the effective frequency range of sEMG signals is
between 20-400 Hz, with components outside this range primar-

fifth-order Butterworth bandpass filter was first applied to the
sEMG signals in both datasets, followed by a 50 Hz notch filter
to eliminate powerline interference. To obtain smoother sEMG
envelope signals for stable model training and faster conver-

low-pass filter were subsequently applied. Finally, since MVC
values were only recorded for the IRASS dataset, sEMG en-
velopes from the IRASS dataset were normalized based on their
respective MVC values, whereas those from the EPIC dataset
were normalized using Z-score normalization. As forjoint angle,
both datasets were smoothed using a fifth-order Butterworth
low-pass filter at 5 Hz, followed by min-max normalization to
linearly scale the wrist and knee joint angle to the ranges of [-1,
1] and [0, 1], respectively.

D. Baseline Models
This study employs eight baseline models, including five
designed for ablation studies on the 3DCNN and TF modules,
and three representative DL models from recent studies. The
five ablation models comprise 3DCNN-Inf, 3DCNN-TFE, and
3DCNN-BM, which sequentially replace the TF module in the
3DCNN-TF with the Inf, TFE, and BM modules, respectively,
as well as the TF and TFE models, where the 3DCNN module
is entirely removed. The other three representative models are
CNN-TFE, CNN-BM, and TCN.
Specifically, the Inf module in 3DCNN-Inf adopts the same
architectural design as in [19]. To achieve optimal predictive
performance, both the encoder and decoder in 3DCNN-Inf are
set to four layers, as validated through multiple experiments.
Each layer utilizes ProbSparse MSA and distillation operations.
Additionally, for a fair comparison, the number of ProbSparse
attention heads and the model dimensions were set to 8 and 256,
respectively, identical to the 3DCNN-TF. The 3DCNN-TFE is
derived from 3DCNN-TF by removing the TFD and autoregres-
sive looping parts, retaining only the positional and segment
encodings, TFE, and FC layers. The TF and TFE replace the
3DCNN module in 3DCNN-TF and 3DCNN-TFE, respectively,
with an embedding layer of
d _ { \mathrm { m o d e l } } = 2 5 6 .
, and their inputs
change from MS features to preprocessed sEMG signals.
As for the representative models, CNN-TFE and CNN-BM
are constructed by replacing the 3DCNN modules in 3DCNN-
TFE and 3DCNN-BM with the three-channel 2DCNN using
conventional
3 \times 3
convolutional kernels, with the number of
channels set to 64, 128, and 256, respectively. Finally, TCN is
modified from the TCN architecture used in the EPIC dataset
[29], comprising three residual blocks with channel sizes of 64,
128, and 256, respectively. Each residual block contains two 1D
causal dilated convolutional layers, with the dilation factors and
kernel sizes being consistent with those in [29].
E. Model Training Settings
To minimize the impact of training environments, all models
were developed and trained using the Pytorch framework on the
Google Colab platform. To ensure reproducibility and fair com-
parisons, identical hyperparameter settings were applied across
all models. Specifically, the AdamW optimizer was employed
for model training, with a batch size of256 and an initial learning
rate set to 0.001. An adaptive learning rate decay strategy was
employed to facilitate model convergence: once the validation
loss plateaued, the learning rate was progressively reduced by
a factor of 0.8. Additionally, the slope of the LeakyReLU acti-
vation function was set to 0.1, and a dropout rate of 20% was
applied to prevent overfitting. All of the above hyperparame-
ter values were determined through iterative experimentation.

D. Baseline Models
This study employs eight baseline models, including five
designed for ablation studies on the 3DCNN and TF modules,
and three representative DL models from recent studies. The
five ablation models comprise 3DCNN-Inf, 3DCNN-TFE, and
3DCNN-BM, which sequentially replace the TF module in the
3DCNN-TF with the Inf, TFE, and BM modules, respectively,
as well as the TF and TFE models, where the 3DCNN module
is entirely removed. The other three representative models are
CNN-TFE, CNN-BM, and TCN.
Specifically, the Inf module in 3DCNN-Inf adopts the same
architectural design as in [19]. To achieve optimal predictive
performance, both the encoder and decoder in 3DCNN-Inf are
set to four layers, as validated through multiple experiments.
Each layer utilizes ProbSparse MSA and distillation operations.
Additionally, for a fair comparison, the number of ProbSparse
attention heads and the model dimensions were set to 8 and 256,
respectively, identical to the 3DCNN-TF. The 3DCNN-TFE is
derived from 3DCNN-TF by removing the TFD and autoregres-
sive looping parts, retaining only the positional and segment
encodings, TFE, and FC layers. The TF and TFE replace the
3DCNN module in 3DCNN-TF and 3DCNN-TFE, respectively,
with an embedding layer of
d _ { \mathrm { m o d e l } } = 2 5 6 .
, and their inputs
change from MS features to preprocessed sEMG signals.
As for the representative models, CNN-TFE and CNN-BM
are constructed by replacing the 3DCNN modules in 3DCNN-
TFE and 3DCNN-BM with the three-channel 2DCNN using
conventional
3 \times 3
convolutional kernels, with the number of
channels set to 64, 128, and 256, respectively. Finally, TCN is
modified from the TCN architecture used in the EPIC dataset

causal dilated convolutional layers, with the dilation factors and
kernel sizes being consistent with those in [29].
E. Model Training Settings
To minimize the impact of training environments, all models
were developed and trained using the Pytorch framework on the
Google Colab platform. To ensure reproducibility and fair com-
parisons, identical hyperparameter settings were applied across
all models. Specifically, the AdamW optimizer was employed
for model training, with a batch size of256 and an initial learning
rate set to 0.001. An adaptive learning rate decay strategy was
employed to facilitate model convergence: once the validation
loss plateaued, the learning rate was progressively reduced by
a factor of 0.8. Additionally, the slope of the LeakyReLU acti-
vation function was set to 0.1, and a dropout rate of 20% was
applied to prevent overfitting. All of the above hyperparame-
ter values were determined through iterative experimentation.
Moreover, to ensure convergence and fair comparisons of train-
ing times, all models were trained for 1000 epochs. The mean
squared error (MSE) between the predicted and true joint angles
was used as the training loss function.
For data partitioning, each subject’s data was randomly di-
vided into 80% for training and 20% for testing. Considering
the limited computational resources of rehabilitation equipment
in practical applications, model training was conducted using an
entry-level NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU, which offers computational
performance comparable to the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2070.
This setup simulates the operational environment of clinical
devices, ensuring practical relevance of the experimental results.

C. Ablation Study of3DCNN-TF
1) 3DCNN Module: The ablation study of the 3DCNN mod-
ule comprises two sets of comparisons. The first compares
3DCNN-TF and 3DCNN-TFE against TF and TFE, while the
second compares 3DCNN-TFE and 3DCNN-BM against CNN-
TFE and CNN-BM. These comparisons collectively demon-
strate the significance of the 3DCNN module and its superiority
over conventional CNNs.
Firstly, compared to TF and TFE, incorporating the additional
3DCNN module not only improved prediction performance by
reducing the average nRMSE by 22%, but also significantly
reduced training time, particularly reducing the average training
time of TF by 75% . Secondly, compared to conventional CNNs,
both 3DCNN-TFE and 3DCNN-BM achieved better prediction
performance and training efficiency, reducing average nRMSE
by 25% and training time by 81% . Moreover, the comparison
between CNN-TFE and TFE further demonstrated that using
conventional CNNs degrades TFE’s prediction performance
while increasing unnecessary training time. This occurs because
conventional CNNs process sEMG images constructed based on
sliding window sizes and electrode channels, where the 3 3 2D
convolution kernel is restricted to extracting only local features
from sEMG images, failing to fully capture MS features from
sEMG images’ spatiotemporal components. Consequently, this
limits the subsequent effectiveness of TFE and BM modules.
In contrast, the 3DCNN module, informed by anatomical
prior knowledge, can efficiently extract MS features from the
raw sEMG. These physiologically interpretable MS features
encapsulate essential motor control information [21]. Therefore,
3DCNN effectively eliminates redundant features and noise
from the raw sEMG, preserving the dynamic spatiotemporal
features of muscle contractions, thereby achieving refinement
and compression of sEMG signals. Additionally, since the pixel
count in each 2D sEMG frame is significantly lower than that of
full sEMG images and the 3DCNN’s convolutional kernels can
cover entire sEMG video segments, the input can be directly
converted into MS features in one step. In contrast, 2DCNN
extracts only local features and requires multiple pooling steps
for effective feature extraction and dimensionality reduction.
Overall, 3DCNN not only substantially reduces computational
complexity during MS feature extraction but also provides more
compact sEMG representations for subsequent TF, TFE, and BM
modules. This facilitates faster training and establishes more
precise contextual dependencies for key MS features in sEMG,
ultimately improving the performance and efficiency.
2) TF Module: The ablation study of the TF module also
consists of two sets of comparisons. The first set compares
3DCNN-TF with other models that also employ the 3DCNN
(3DCNN-InF, 3DCNN-TFE, and 3DCNN-BM), while the sec-
ond compares TF with TFE. These comparisons collectively
validate the necessity of employing the complete TF structure.
The first comparison demonstrates that, compared to using
InF, TFE, or BM following the 3DCNN, 3DCNN-TF reduced
the average nRMSE by 15.2%, 19.9%, and 23.5%, respectively.
The second comparison shows that the advantage of TFD does
not fully rely on the quality of the input features. Even without
the MS features provided by 3DCNN, TF still outperformed
TFE, reducing the average nRMSE by 5.7% . These significant
improvements stem from three key advantages of the complete
TF architecture over InF, TFE, and BM: the complete MSA,
autoregressive generation, and MCA.
Firstly, joint angle prediction from sEMG is a short-term time
series forecasting task that requires capturing high-frequency
dynamics and fine-grained features in sEMG. However, InF,
which is designed for long-term sequence prediction, fails to
fully exploit its strengths in this context. This limitation arises
because InF sacrifices accuracy for computational efficiency in
long-term forecasting, with its ProbSparse MSA and distillation
operations based on the max pooling losing critical contex-
tual relationships among MS features. In contrast, TF’s MSA
captures complete global contextual dependencies within MS
feature sequences, preserving all essential MS information. This
is further evidenced by the model depth, where the single-layer
TF achieves higher predictive accuracy than the four-layer InF.
Additionally, the autoregressive generation of TF, as opposed
to InF’s one-shot generation, dynamically adjusts the prediction
strategy by utilizing historical information, thereby correcting
deviations and ensuring the temporal coherence and stability of
the TFD outputs. Therefore, 3DCNN-TF balances accuracy and
computational efficiency more effectively than 3DCNN-InF.
Secondly, apart from autoregressive generation, comparisons
between TF and TFE further highlights the importance of MCA.
MCA enables TFD to dynamically screen key MS information
provided by TFE that is most relevant to the next joint angle
prediction based on cross-sequence contextual dependencies be-
tween current sEMG signals and historical joint angles, thereby
accurately generating the joint angle for the next step.
Lastly, the comparison between TF and BM further validates
the integrated effect of the three key advantages of TF. Since
BM’s MSA is built atop BiLSTM, it is constrained by BiLSTM’s
recurrent structure, limiting its ability to establish long-range
contextual dependencies within the feature sequences, thereby
degrading prediction performance. In contrast, TF can model
contextual dependencies across arbitrary temporal spans in par-
allel and mitigate gradient vanishing or explosion issues inherent
in BiLSTM. Nonetheless, these advantages of TF come at the
cost of reduced computational efficiency.

E. Limitations and Future Work
The two datasets and the proposed 3DCNN-TF model in this
study still have several limitations. Regarding the dataset, future
studies should incorporate more joint types, multi-degree-of-
freedom joint movements, more subjects, and longer durations
of randomized and complex movements, to comprehensively
evaluate the robustness and generalizability of the model. Ad-
ditionally, future work should include stroke patients and test
3DCNN-TF’s real-time prediction capability to ensure its relia-
bility in actual non-standardized rehabilitation scenarios.
Regarding the 3DCNN-TF model, in addition to reducing
its reliance on the precise positioning of target muscles and
sEMG electrodes during 2D sEMG frame reconstruction, it
is also essential to improve the training efficiency of the TF
module without losing performance. Therefore, future work
could integrate explicit spatial synergy encoding based on polar
coordinates, as proposed in [36], wherein electrode phase differ-
ences encode relative spatial relationships of muscle activation,
thereby improving 3DCNN’s MS extraction and robustness
against electrode shift. Moreover, other TF variants can be con-
sidered to reduce the computational complexity of MSA, MCA,
and FFN. Additionally, the DL-based 3DCNN-TF inherently
functions as a black-box tool, lacking interpretability regarding
the neurophysiological mechanisms between sEMG and joint
kinematics. Hence, future research could integrate MSK-based
motion equations into the current MSE loss function as an
additional constraint. Moreover, 3DCNN-TF could serve as the
generator network, while the multi-joint hierarchical optimized
Hill model from [37] could act as the discriminator network
in a GAN framework. This approach would leverage MSK
biomechanical priors during adversarial training to enhance both
interpretability and multi-joint coordination prediction capabil-
ities of the model, while also reducing its reliance on large-scale
training datasets. Furthermore, 3DCNN-TF can be extended
into a multimodal fusion framework that integrates sEMG and
IMU signals to improve prediction accuracy. In addition, the
model can be pre-trained on large-scale datasets to extract both
subject-invariant and subject-specific MS components, followed
by subject-specific fine-tuning to enable rapid few-shot transfer
learning.
VI. CONCLUSION
For the first time, this study redefines the problem of motion
intention prediction from the perspective ofSeq2Seq translation,
achieving an accurate translation from neural control signals to
kinematic representation by analogizing sEMG and joint angles
as the source and target languages, respectively. Specifically,
the model input is reformulated into a “sentence” formed by
stacking multiple sEMG sliding windows, where each sliding
window serves as a “word” within the “sentence.” This design
enables the model to capture more comprehensive temporal

Firstly, the 3DCNN module reconstructs each “sentence” into
sEMG video segments based on the anatomical distribution
and electrode placement of the target muscles, thereby extract-
ing MS features that represent the essence of neural control.
This significantly enhances the model’s prediction accuracy
while substantially reducing training time. Subsequently, the TF
module dynamically captures global contextual dependencies
between MS feature sequences and joint angle sequences from
multiple perspectives through the synergistic effects of TFE,
TFD, and autoregressive generation loop, ultimately generating
precise joint angle predictions as translation results step by step.
Experimental results on two datasets involving wrist and
knee flexion/extension tasks indicate that 3DCNN-TF achieves
optimal overall performance compared to eight baseline models,
striking an optimal balance between prediction accuracy and
computational efficiency while exhibiting superior robustness
and generalizability. Additionally, 3DCNN-TF can predict joint
angles up to 300 ms in advance without loss of accuracy, high-
lighting its potential in real-time rehabilitation assistance.

thereby achieving precise prediction from sEMG to joint angles.
Firstly, the 3DCNN module reconstructs each “sentence” into
sEMG video segments based on the anatomical distribution
and electrode placement of the target muscles, thereby extract-
ing MS features that represent the essence of neural control.
This significantly enhances the model’s prediction accuracy
while substantially reducing training time. Subsequently, the TF
module dynamically captures global contextual dependencies
between MS feature sequences and joint angle sequences from
multiple perspectives through the synergistic effects of TFE,
TFD, and autoregressive generation loop, ultimately generating
precise joint angle predictions as translation results step by step.
Experimental results on two datasets involving wrist and
knee flexion/extension tasks indicate that 3DCNN-TF achieves
optimal overall performance compared to eight baseline models,
striking an optimal balance between prediction accuracy and
computational efficiency while exhibiting superior robustness
and generalizability. Additionally, 3DCNN-TF can predict joint
angles up to 300 ms in advance without loss of accuracy, high-
lighting its potential in real-time rehabilitation assistance.
